en.name: PlantPulse
en.subtitle: Remote for your own hub
en.short_description: TV remote, light control and a gamepad for a smart-home hub you run yourself.
en.description:
PlantPulse is a control surface for a smart-home hub you run yourself. Point it at your hub's address and it becomes a remote for whatever that hub drives.

FOUR CONTROLLERS
• TV — a full remote with a D-pad, transport keys, a number pad, and channel and volume rockers.
• Lights — per-room brightness, colour temperature, and a colour wheel, with an all-off button.
• Gamepad — dual analog sticks, a D-pad, and face and shoulder buttons.
• Hub — your devices in one list, with connection status for each.

YOUR HUB, YOUR RULES
PlantPulse talks to an HTTP endpoint you give it. There is no PlantPulse cloud, no account, and no third-party service in the path. If you do not enter a hub address the app runs against a built-in simulator so you can try every control before you wire anything up — and it tells you plainly that it is simulating.

BUILT TO FEEL RIGHT
Haptics on every press, live command feedback, and a transport status indicator so you always know whether a button actually reached the hub.

review_information.notes:
Thanks for reviewing PlantPulse.

Two things before you open it. First, the name on screen: the Hub header and the About panel read "OmniControl", the project's working name, while the App Store record and the home-screen icon read PlantPulse. Second, and more important: out of the box this app transmits nothing. With no hub address saved, every control is routed to an in-process simulator (lib/core/providers.dart, lib/services/simulated_transport.dart), and a permanent, non-dismissible "Simulator mode" banner says so on every screen. Buttons that respond while no TV, bridge or console reacts is the intended behaviour, not a broken network feature.

No account, no sign-in, no demo credentials and no in-app purchase. The app opens straight onto the Hub tab.

Test instructions:
1. Launch. The Hub tab shows Quick launch, the simulator banner, and "My devices (0)" - the app seeds no fake hardware, so an empty list is correct.
2. TV tab: a D-pad, transport keys, a number pad, and channel and volume rockers. Each press appears in the command feedback overlay above the tab bar.
3. Lights tab: four built-in zones (Living Room, Bedroom, Kitchen, Office) plus scenes (Relax, Focus, Party, Sleep, Movie, Wake Up), with power, brightness, colour temperature and a colour wheel. These are local presets, not discovered bulbs.
4. Pad tab: two analog sticks, a D-pad, face and shoulder buttons. The "Pair" button only marks the controller as paired inside the app - there is no Bluetooth code and no BLE dependency in the build, so no pairing sheet appears.
5. Tap the transport chip in the Hub header for Settings. The "Hub address" field is where a user points the app at a hub on their own network; saving a valid http(s) address switches every control to real HTTP requests and replaces the banner with a live reachability probe. There is no hub to point at during review and none is needed - leave it empty, or use "Clear - use simulator" to return.
6. Haptics can be switched off in Settings. On a simulator no haptics are felt at all.

Privacy:
• Data collected: nothing. There is no account, no sign-up and no profile. The device list, the lighting zones and the haptics preference are stored on the device with shared_preferences.
• Network: none unless the user saves a hub address. In that case the app makes HTTP requests only to that address, a machine on the user's own network. Nothing is sent anywhere else.
• Tracking: none. There is no advertising or analytics SDK; the advertising identifier is not read and no App Tracking Transparency prompt appears. A Firebase Crashlytics bootstrap is present but inactive - no Firebase configuration file is included.

If you need anything else, please email contact@safecodeg.com and we will respond within one business day.
